claim_verdicts.evidence: Settled by inspection, not execution: `dotnet` and `git` could not be run in this session (command approval denied), so the claim is verified from the stage-0 source, which is deterministic. Run() contains exactly two statements: `Console.WriteLine($"expected 2150000, got {TotalVnd(orderOne)}");` and `Console.WriteLine($"one line only: expected 1250000, got {TotalVnd(orderOne[..1])}");`. With orderOne = {(1,1250000),(2,450000)} the values are 1250000 and 0 (claims 7-10). Int32 default formatting has no group separator in any culture.

WrongTotal.cs line 4 records 900.000; the sample's first line prints 1250000 (claim 10), so the reported figure is not produced by this code at stage-0. seed.sql line 38 gives order 1's second row as 2 x 450000 = 900000, which is exactly the reported figure, i.e. the sum of the order's last line alone. Arithmetic only; no document needed.

C# language reference, iteration statements, the `for` statement: "The *initializer* section that executes only once, before entering the loop." and "The *condition* section that determines if the next iteration in the loop should run. If it evaluates to `true` or isn't present, the next iteration runs. Otherwise, the loop exits." The first iteration is a "next iteration", so with lines.Count == 1 the condition `0 < 0` is false on its first evaluation and the body never runs.

WrongTotal.cs: `var totalVnd = 0;` (line 9), the only write to it is `totalVnd += lines[i].Quantity * lines[i].UnitPriceVnd;` (line 12) inside the loop body, and `return totalVnd;` (line 15) is the only return. If the body never runs, the returned value is the initial 0.

C# language reference, member access operators, Range operator `..`: "The left-hand operand is an *inclusive* start of a range. The right-hand operand is an *exclusive* end of a range.", "`..b` is equivalent to `0..b`" and the table row "`..end` | Values from the start to the `end` exclusively." Also: "Single dimensional arrays are *countable*." orderOne is a single-dimensional array, so `orderOne[..1]` is indices 0..1 exclusive — the first element only.

orderOne has 2 elements (WrongTotal.cs line 20), so `lines.Count - 1` is 1: i = 0 passes `0 < 1` and the body adds 1 * 1250000; i = 1 fails `1 < 1` and the loop exits, leaving 2 * 450000 = 900000 out. TotalVnd returns 1250000 where the order's true total is 2150000 (claim 2). Condition-before-each-iteration is claim 7's documented behaviour.

With lines.Count == 3, `lines.Count - 1` is 2: i takes 0 and 1, adding 1 * 1250000 and 2 * 450000 = 2150000, and stops before the third item, 1 * 320000. Correct total 2150000 + 320000 = 2470000. 320000 is a real price in the data (db/seed.sql line 10, product 5 'Gia do laptop', 320000), so the invented third line is consistent with the repository.
claim_verdicts.source: examples/don-hang @ stage-0: WrongTotal.cs:10-12 evaluated at Count = 3; db/seed.sql:10

claim_verdicts.evidence: Tautological given the lesson's own definition of a reproduction in section 3 ("produces the same failure every time"): with no run that failed before the change, no run after it can be a comparison. No official document governs this. Documents opened for this claim: none applicable — dotnet-run.md and the C# language reference say nothing about debugging method.

Method heuristic, not documented behaviour, and the lesson now carries both branches: "If it survives, the half you kept is enough to trigger it, so keep halving there. If it disappears, what you removed matters, so put half of it back and run again." The claim text matches that prose; neither branch over-claims under the lesson's premise that the failure appears on demand.

The ledger text over-reaches in two places. (a) "removes one possible cause whether it survives or not": the lesson says it only for the disproved branch — "a disproved sentence still removes one possible cause"; a surviving hypothesis removes nothing, it survives. (b) The lesson's absolute "A check whose result you cannot predict decides nothing." is true only of the sentence under test; an unpredicted run can still produce information. Nothing in the dotnet or C# documentation governs either half.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: A hypothesis is one sentence a single check could show to be false, with the check's result predicted beforehand so that it decides that sentence either way; a disproved sentence removes one possible cause, and changing code before any sentence is on the table cannot be distinguished from guessing.

claim_verdicts.evidence: The lesson says only: "The notes grow the whole way through, and they are what a later question or written report is made of." The ledger's added cost comparison — "keeping it during the session costs less than reconstructing it afterwards" — appears nowhere in the lesson and has no source; it is an unmeasured claim about effort. The supportable half is the one the lesson actually makes.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: Opinion: the running record of what you ran, what you expected and what you got is what a later question or written report is made of.

claim_verdicts.evidence: The inference is stated as a proof ("the only way"), and it is offered before the reader has seen TotalVnd's body — output is all they hold. From a printed 0 alone, other causes survive: a body that ran and added a zero term, an early `return 0`, a loop reading a different index. It is true only because this function has one accumulator and exactly one write (WrongTotal.cs:9-15), which is precisely what the next paragraph's check is meant to establish rather than assume.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: Of the two printed lines the 0 is the easier to explain, because for this input — a single line of 1 x 1.250.000 — the simplest explanation for a sum that stays 0 is a loop body that never ran, while 1.250.000 is a plausible number that still needs explaining.

claim_verdicts.evidence: Stated in the lesson with its own limit attached ("often lives in the gap", and the claim adds "Not all bugs are of this kind"), so it is a hedged observation, not a rule to be sourced. No official document covers how humans re-read code. Documents opened while reviewing this lesson: refs/dotnet-docs dotnet-run.md, iteration-statements.md, member-access-operators.md.

dotnet-run.md, Options: "**`--project <PATH>`** Specifies the path of the project file to run (folder name or full path). If not specified, it defaults to the current directory." Synopsis: "[--project <PATH>]". Example: "dotnet run --project ./projects/proj1/proj1.csproj". The lesson's "`--project` names the project to run — here the folder that holds it" is inside what the option accepts.

issues.text: Unlisted claim. Claim 6 covers only "the reported figure is not reproducible at stage-0"; the clause after "so" is a separate, unconditioned rule — when your run disagrees with the report, work on your number instead. It contradicts the lesson's own definition in section 3 (a reproduction "produces the same failure every time"): a run printing 1250000 does not reproduce a report of 900.000, and the lesson never says the two may be different failures. A junior taught this will close reports that were never reproduced.
issues.quote: You cannot reproduce the reported number from this code, so the number you produce yourself is the one to explain.
issues.fix: Condition it and list it: "…so this run does not reproduce the report. Record the gap — the reporter's input, data or version may differ — and explain the failure you can produce while you go back and ask for theirs." Add that sentence to .meta.json claims as kind `opinion`, section 5.

issues.text: An absolute ("the only way") asserted from output alone, before the reader has been shown the loop body. A printed 0 is also consistent with a body that ran and added a zero term, an early `return 0`, or a loop reading the wrong index. The sentence holds only because this particular function has one accumulator and one write — which is what the check in the next paragraph is supposed to establish, not assume.
issues.quote: the only way the sum stays 0 is a loop body that never ran
issues.fix: Replace "the only way the sum stays 0 is" with "the simplest explanation for a sum that stays 0 is", leaving it a hypothesis the following check confirms. Update claim 16 in .meta.json to the same wording.

issues.text: An absolute with no scope. An unpredicted check can still produce information — a printed value, a crash, a timing — what it cannot do is decide the sentence you are holding, which is the point the paragraph is making.
issues.quote: A check whose result you cannot predict decides nothing.
issues.fix: Add the scope: "A check whose result you cannot predict decides nothing about the sentence you are testing."
